demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 31, a Middle Eastern woman who works as a social media manager for a small lifestyle brand, and when she tells her story she always begins with the moment before everything changed. It is early evening, the end of a long workday spent scheduling posts, answering comments, and rushing through revisions for a campaign launch. She is driving home with her phone on the passenger seat, still vibrating every few minutes with notifications she feels responsible for answering. At a red light, she glances down, just for a second, to read a message from her boss asking whether a sponsored post has gone live. When she looks up, traffic has started moving. She presses the gas, distracted, and does not see the pedestrian stepping into the crosswalk until the impact has already happened.

She remembers the sound more than the image: a dull, sickening thud that does not seem real at first. Then there is screaming, her own and someone else’s. She stumbles out of the car and sees a man on the pavement, twisted in a way she cannot understand. In her memory everything after that comes in fragments—her hands shaking so hard she drops her phone while trying to call 911, strangers gathering around, someone shouting at her to back away, the metallic smell in the air, the flashing lights. At the hospital, police ask her questions she can barely process. She keeps saying, “I didn’t see him. I didn’t see him,” as if repetition might undo what happened. The man survives, but with serious injuries. She learns later that he faces multiple surgeries and a long rehabilitation. That fact does not comfort her. In some ways it makes things worse. He is alive, and therefore still living every day with what she did.

In the first weeks afterward, she does not sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. Each time she closes her eyes, she sees the crosswalk and the body hitting the hood of her car. Sometimes the image comes with full sensory force, as if she is back inside the vehicle with her foot frozen on the pedal. She starts waking in panic, drenched in sweat, her heart racing so hard she sits upright and checks the room to remind herself where she is. During the day, the sound of a horn or the sight of a crosswalk makes her stomach drop. At work, she stares at her screen and suddenly loses track of what campaign she is building because she is back at the accident scene, hearing sirens.

Before the accident, she prides herself on being quick, responsive, always available. Her job rewards constant attention to notifications, trends, and performance metrics. Afterward, every ping of her phone feels accusatory. She begins to read messages and then put the phone down, unable to answer. She misses deadlines. When she has to schedule posts about cheerful things—vacations, beauty products, holiday sales—she feels almost offended by the brightness of the images. She thinks, absurdly but persistently, that she should not be allowed to make anything look attractive again. She has caused irreversible harm; the world should not expect her to return to captions and engagement reports as though nothing happened.

She avoids driving whenever she can. At first she tells people she is being environmentally conscious or trying to save money on gas, but in reality she cannot bear to sit behind the wheel. If she has no choice, she grips it so tightly her hands ache. At every intersection she slows excessively, scanning sidewalks and crosswalks over and over. If a pedestrian is anywhere nearby, her chest tightens and she feels a rush of heat through her body. More than once she has had to pull over because she becomes dizzy and sure she is about to crash again. She starts taking longer routes just to avoid the street where the accident happened.

The guilt settles into her marriage like a third person in the room. Her husband initially tries to reassure her that she made a mistake, that she is not a monster, but she cannot hear that without feeling he is minimizing what happened. She grows irritable and withdrawn. When he touches her unexpectedly, she startles violently and then feels ashamed. He says she is never really present anymore. She says he has no idea what it is like to live with the knowledge that someone’s life was shattered because she looked at a message about work. Over time their conversations become flatter, then sharper, then sparse. By the time the divorce is finalized, she describes feeling as if she has already been emotionally absent for months.

Now, more than a year later, her life has narrowed. She still works, mostly from home, where she can control the noise and avoid commuting. She keeps her camera off during meetings because she worries people will see the exhaustion on her face. She scans local news compulsively, terrified she will come across an update about the injured man and equally terrified she will not. In quiet moments she imagines his daily life—how he gets out of bed, whether he still works, whether he hates her. She rarely sees friends. When family members encourage her to move on, she becomes silent, because “moving on” feels to her like betrayal.

What stands out most is how trapped she feels between memory and responsibility. She does not talk about the accident as a past event. She talks about it as something still happening, over and over, in flashes, in dreams, in the tightening of her hands around a steering wheel, in every phone notification that lights up beside her. She lives as if one moment of distraction has divided her life permanently into before and after, and she no longer trusts herself to belong fully to the world she used to move through so easily.
